# Spherical Harmonics Optimization

Also called: SH Optimization, SH Distillation, SH Quantization, Camera Jacobian Derivation, Multi-View Training Efficiency

## Overview
This family encompasses methods that optimize the appearance representation, training stability, and computational efficiency of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) by modifying how Spherical Harmonics (SH) coefficients are initialized, compressed, distilled, or how the underlying optimization loop handles gradients and camera poses. It addresses the high memory cost of high-degree SH, the instability of single-view gradient variance, and the computational overhead of automatic differentiation in SLAM contexts. It differs from sibling methods like [DAVIGS](12021-davigs.md) and [3iGS](13977-3igs-factorised-tensorial-illumination-for-3d-gaussian-splat.md) by focusing on coefficient reduction, quantization, and training infrastructure rather than factorizing the illumination model itself.

## Shared principles
All methods in this family operate on the standard 3DGS rendering equation, where the pixel color $\hat{\mathbf{C}}$ is computed via alpha-blending of Gaussian contributions:
$$ \hat{\mathbf{C}} = \sum_{i \in N} T_i g_i(\mathbf{u} | \boldsymbol{\mu}', \boldsymbol{\Sigma}') \alpha_i \mathbf{c}_i(\omega) $$
where $T_i$ is transmittance, $g_i$ is the 2D Gaussian density, $\alpha_i$ is opacity, and $\mathbf{c}_i(\omega)$ is the view-dependent outgoing radiance. The core variation across methods lies in the definition and optimization of $\mathbf{c}_i(\omega)$ and potentially $\alpha_i$, moving beyond the fixed Spherical Harmonics (SH) coefficients $\mathbf{c}_i$ used in base 3DGS.

## Subtopics

### [First-order Spherical Harmonics Distillation](9467-first-order-spherical-harmonics-distillation.md)
First-order Spherical Harmonics Distillation reduces the spherical harmonics (SH) degree of 3D Gaussian elements from third-order to first-order to decrease parameter count and computation cost. It achieves this by distilling the appearance information from a high-fidelity teacher model (using third-order SH) into a lower-dimensional student model (using first-order SH). Unlike standard degree reduction which may suffer from significant quality loss, this method uses knowledge distillation to preserve rendering fidelity while enabling faster rendering and lower storage usage, making it suitable for mobile and edge hardware deployment. See [First-order Spherical Harmonics Distillation](9467-first-order-spherical-harmonics-distillation.md).

### [Explicit Camera Jacobian Derivation](10077-explicit-camera-jacobian-derivation.md)
This method derives analytical Jacobians of the SE(3) camera pose with respect to 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) primitives to enable efficient camera pose optimization in SLAM systems. It solves the problem of high computational overhead associated with automatic differentiation during gradient descent tracking by providing minimal, closed-form derivatives on the Lie group manifold. Unlike prior ray-intersection methods that assume fewer Gaussians, this approach is specifically designed for the EWA splatting rasterization used in 3DGS, ensuring dimensionality matches the six degrees of freedom of the camera pose. See [Explicit Camera Jacobian Derivation](10077-explicit-camera-jacobian-derivation.md).

### [Efficient Multi-View Training for 3D Gaussian Splatting](13982-efficient-multi-view-training-for-3d-gaussian-splatting.md)
This method enables stable optimization of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) by training on multiple views per iteration, addressing the high variance of gradients inherent in the standard single-view approach. It overcomes the rasterization overhead and adaptive density control (ADC) incompatibilities of naive multi-view rendering through thread-efficient partial rendering and 3D-space loss computation. See [Efficient Multi-View Training for 3D Gaussian Splatting](13982-efficient-multi-view-training-for-3d-gaussian-splatting.md).

### [Spherical Harmonics Vector Quantization](14181-spherical-harmonics-vector-quantization.md)
Spherical Harmonics Vector Quantization (SH VQ) is a compression technique for 3D Gaussian Splatting that replaces the continuous per-splat SH coefficients with discrete indices pointing to a shared, finite palette of distinct SH vectors. This method significantly reduces the memory footprint of the scene representation by trading minor lighting artifacts for substantial storage savings, making it suitable for constrained environments such as real-time web or mobile rendering. Unlike dimensionality reduction methods that lower the SH degree, SH VQ retains the full high-frequency detail capacity of the original SH basis but approximates the specific coefficients using a limited set of prototypes. See [Spherical Harmonics Vector Quantization](14181-spherical-harmonics-vector-quantization.md).

#### SH Degree Zero Optimization
- **Definition**: Setting the maximum degree of Spherical Harmonics (SH) coefficients to 0 to remove superfluous operations and improve training speed, as higher-degree SH coefficients for color remain unchanged during training [S1, unofficial].
- **Step**: Modify the model code to delete operations relative to the max degree in the model and set the max degree parameter to 0 [S1, unofficial].
- **Pitfall**: In the original 3D Gaussian Splatting model, features represented by SH coefficients with degree > 0 are unchanged during all training, making them useless [S1, unofficial].
- **Numbers**: Directly changing the max degree to 0 yields a 16.25% improvement compared to the default. With specific changing code, it yields a 16.57% improvement but increases CPU-GPU process time [S1, unofficial].

## Background
The base 3D Gaussian Splatting method [12] uses third-order SH (48 coefficients per Gaussian) to represent view-dependent color. Subsequent research identified inefficiencies in this representation. [S1, unofficial] observed that higher-degree SH coefficients for color remain unchanged during training, suggesting that degree 0 optimization can improve speed without quality loss. Other works addressed the memory bottleneck of high-degree SH through distillation [S2, unofficial] and vector quantization [S1, unofficial], while SLAM applications required analytical Jacobians [S1, unofficial] to replace expensive automatic differentiation. Multi-view training strategies were also developed to stabilize gradient variance [S1, unofficial].
